content: After more than six decades of failed attempts, chemists have achieved a breakthrough involving a class of molecules long considered too unstable to isolate. Chemists have succeeded in isolating a group of molecules that researchers have struggled to capture for more than 60 years. Known as oxoboranes, these compounds contain an unusual triple bond between boron and oxygen, a combination long considered too unstable to isolate in a lasting form. Researchers led by Professor Holger Braunschweig at the University of Würzburg have now developed a method that produces three surprisingly stable oxoboranes. Published in Nature Chemistry , the work was supported by computational research from Professor Ashwini K. Phukan’s team at Tezpur University in India. The breakthrough began when Würzburg doctoral students Lukas Lubczyk and Christian Markl independently reacted a compound called a diboracumulene with different ketones, chemicals commonly used in organic synthesis. Instead of the anticipated products, they obtained unusual orange or yellow solids. The reactions had unexpectedly produced oxoboranes as their main products. “The discovery was a pleasant surprise. I never thought the diboracumulene would react the way it did, let alone with multiple different, simple substrates. And when Christian came to me with his compound, I knew we were onto something,” says Lukas Lubczyk. Boron has a strong tendency to avoid forming triple bonds, making these molecules particularly difficult to synthesize. Braunschweig has spent more than 15 years investigating this type of chemical bonding. His team created the first molecule containing a boron-boron triple bond in 2012, followed by the first neutral molecule with a boron-carbon triple bond in 2025. Organic oxoboranes represented the remaining challenge involving triple bonds between boron and other elements in the first row of the periodic table’s p-block. Chemists have pursued oxoboranes since at least the early 1960s. Although previous experiments detected or trapped them under extreme conditions, inferred their presence from chemical reactions, or produced related derivatives, researchers had been unable to isolate stable examples. “Nearly everybody in the field had given up on oxoboranes, as they were thought to be just too unstable to be isolated. So we were stunned to see them spontaneously form in these reactions and stick around long enough that we could study them,” says Holger Braunschweig. The successful preparation of three oxoboranes suggests that the new approach could provide access to additional members of this difficult-to-synthesize molecular family. The researchers are now investigating whether the method can be extended to produce other elusive compounds involving elements across the periodic table. Reference: “Synthesis and isolation of stable oxoboranes” by Lukas Lubczyk, Christian Markl, Mudit Jain, Sourav Kar, Thomas Kupfer, Rian D. Dewhurst, Ashwini K. Phukan and Holger Braunschweig, 27 October 2026, Nature Chemistry . DOI: 10.1038/s41557-026-02272-w The work was funded by the German Research Foundation (DFG), the German Academic Exchange Service (DAAD) and the Department of Science & Technology (DST) of India. content: A breakthrough in brain-inspired electronics could lead to devices that process information and learn without relying on conventional computing architectures. A single nanoscale electronic component can perform three different jobs, switching electrical current, storing information through resistance, and remembering past electrical activity through changes in capacitance. Researchers in Germany have demonstrated this versatility using unusual oxide materials, opening a possible path toward computer hardware that processes information and adapts more like the human brain. Today’s artificial intelligence systems can consume enormous amounts of electricity, particularly during the training of large models. One reason researchers are exploring alternative hardware is that conventional computers typically separate memory from computation, requiring information to move between them. The brain operates differently. Its neurons communicate through synapses, connections that can change in response to repeated or intense signals. This ability to adapt, known as neuroplasticity, helps the brain learn from experience. A research team at the University of Würzburg, working within the Würzburg and Dresden Cluster of Excellence ctd.qmat, has developed electronic components that reproduce several important behaviors of neurons and synapses. Their approach uses complex oxides, materials whose electrical properties can be adjusted to support different functions within the same system. The devices rely on two materials: lanthanum aluminate (LaAlO₃, or LAO for short) and strontium titanate (SrTiO₃, or STO for short). Both are electrical insulators individually, but when brought together, they form an extremely thin conductive layer at their interface. This layer, called a quasi-two-dimensional electron gas, allows electrons to move through a region confined to the boundary between the materials. By carefully patterning the interface, researchers can create microscopic conductive pathways, sometimes described as “electron highways.” Electrical current can displace oxygen atoms within the structure, altering its resistance. These changes allow the device to be “trained” through electrical stimulation, providing a physical mechanism for storing information about previous activity. Using this material platform, the Würzburg researchers created components that can act as a transistor, a memristor, or a memcapacitor. A transistor controls current flow, while a memristor stores information through changes in electrical resistance. A memcapacitor behaves differently: its ability to store electrical charge depends on its previous electrical state. The researchers demonstrated that a single nanoscale component can provide any of these three functions depending on how it is connected electrically. This versatility could simplify the design of artificial neural networks built directly into electronic hardware. “What makes our platform so exciting is that we can realize very different functions using the same material system. This brings us closer to hardware that not only computes but can also learn directly within the component and temporarily store information,” says Soumen Pradhan, a postdoctoral researcher at the Chair of Technical Physics in Würzburg. “Brain-inspired computing” seeks to reproduce some of the brain’s information processing and learning mechanisms in electronic circuits. Rather than continually transferring data between separate processing and memory units, these systems aim to combine computation, information storage, and adaptation within individual components. “Complex oxides are an especially exciting field for us because they combine many electronic properties in a single material platform. That is precisely what makes them so interesting for a new generation of energy-efficient and adaptable computer hardware,” says Ralph Claessen, spokesperson at JMU Würzburg for the Würzburg–Dresden Cluster of Excellence ctd.qmat and a co-author of the study. One potential application is health monitoring. Wearable devices incorporating this type of adaptive electronics might eventually analyze physiological signals directly, without requiring separate computing hardware for every processing task. Such “self-learning” sensors could potentially track heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, blood oxygen saturation, or blood glucose while adapting their responses to incoming data. Processing signals locally could also reduce the energy required to transfer information to external systems. For now, these possibilities remain long-term goals. The research demonstrates the underlying electronic functions rather than a complete artificial intelligence system or medical sensor. Further development will be needed to establish whether the technology can deliver practical improvements in energy consumption, reliability, and performance. Reference: “Oxide interface-based polymorphic electronic devices for neuromorphic computing” by Soumen Pradhan, Kirill Miller, Fabian Hartmann, Merit Spring, Judith Gabel, Berengar Leikert, Silke Kuhn, Martin Kamp, Victor Lopez-Richard, Michael Sing, Ralph Claessen and Sven Höfling, 9 April 2026, Nature Communications . content: Einstein’s equations suggest that gravity may be capable of a process resembling the one behind powerful solar explosions. In a new theoretical study, physicists show how gravitational field structures can change their connections and transfer energy into matter. They call this process “gravitational reconnection.” Luca Comisso of Columbia University and Felipe A. Asenjo of Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez in Chile describe the discovery in Physical Review D . Their work reveals a mathematical connection between gravity and the behavior of plasmas, electrically charged gases found in stars and throughout space. In plasmas, magnetic field lines can become stretched and twisted until they rearrange through a process called “magnetic reconnection.” This releases stored magnetic energy and drives powerful events such as solar flares. “Magnetic reconnection is when these field lines, in some specific configuration, break and reattach in a different configuration,” Comisso said. “When they break and reconnect, they release energy.” He added, “It takes energy from the magnetic field and gives it to the particles in the plasma, producing explosions, energetic events.” Gravity operates differently because Einstein’s theory describes space-time as a four-dimensional structure rather than three-dimensional space. “Because space-time is four-dimensional rather than three-dimensional, gravity involves something like field ‘sheets’ rather than field lines,” explained Comisso. “Adding one dimension to a line gives you a plane. You can think of it as putting many lines together to form a ‘sheet.’” These sheets are mathematical structures, not physical surfaces. The researchers found that when the conditions preserving their connections break down, the sheets can reconnect, allowing energy to transfer from the gravitational field into matter. The researchers uncovered this behavior by expressing Einstein’s equations using different mathematical variables, revealing similarities with equations that describe plasmas. Their study builds on earlier research with Maricarmen A. Winkler that identified previously unrecognized constraints on how space-time can evolve. “Einstein’s equations contain constraints on how space-time can evolve that are not immediately apparent,” said Asenjo. “By revealing these hidden new properties, we can begin to understand the fundamental rules governing how this gravitational reconnection process behaves.” “Some implications are hidden in the equations, and they are not straightforward to capture just by looking at them,” Comisso said. “You need to rewrite them in a different way, and then you can exploit that behavior.” One potential application involves merging black holes, where extreme gravity severely distorts space-time. Scientists rely on powerful computer simulations to predict the gravitational waves produced by these collisions, which detectors such as the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO) are designed to measure. The newly identified constraints could help researchers determine how gravitational fields must behave without calculating every detail of their evolution. “It helps us predict some patterns of the space-time,” Comisso said. “Even without doing the full calculation, we know that space-time needs to behave in a certain way, that it needs to satisfy those constraints.” Gravitational reconnection remains a theoretical discovery. Researchers must now investigate whether it occurs in astrophysical environments, how much energy it could transfer, and whether it might produce detectable signatures in gravitational waves. Reference: “Reconnection of gravitational fields” by Luca Comisso and Felipe A. Asenjo, 28 October 2026, Physical Review D . DOI: 10.1103/lmqy-pf9k The research was supported by the National Science Foundation and NASA. Never miss a breakthrough: Join the SciTechDaily newsletter. Follow us on Google and Google News .
